The bar was called the Lantern, though the bulb had been dead for years and the “light” came from a string of candles someone had strung along the back shelf. Mara and Jonah sat on stools too close together, the way they had since they were twelve.

“You always said the lake house was mine,” Jonah said.

“It was mine,” Mara said. “You were the one who stole the key.”

“I borrowed it.”

“You stole it.”

He laughed, but it came out thin. He’d had three beers, maybe four. Mara had two and a half, which was enough to make her voice sound like it belonged to someone braver.

“You remember it wrong,” she said.

“I remember it exactly. You were crying in the bathroom because your dad was yelling. I went in and told you to stop. You said I was a coward.”

“I said you were a coward because you were scared of him.”

“I was scared of the water.”

“You were scared of everything.”

“That’s not the same as being a coward.”

Mara turned her glass in a slow circle. “You were the one who told your mom I was the one who broke the window.”

“I didn’t lie.”

“You lied.”

“I said you were the one who was there.”

“That’s a lie.”

“It was the truth. You were there.”

The bartender, who had stopped pretending to care, refilled Jonah’s glass without asking. Mara watched the candlelight flicker across his face. He looked older than she remembered, but also smaller, like the version of him she’d known had been left behind somewhere in the dark.

“You know what I remember?” she said. “The night your dad left. You were sitting on the porch with your shoes off. You were crying. I didn’t say anything because I was scared you’d hate me.”

“You didn’t hate me.”

“I was scared.”

“You were scared of me.”

“I was scared of everything.”

He looked at her then, and for a second the drunk edge dropped away. “You were the only one who stayed,” he said.

“You were the one who stayed.”

“I stayed because I was scared.”

“You stayed because you cared.”

“Maybe both.”

The argument had been circling the same wound for an hour. Mara felt the old sting of it, the way childhood memories could feel less like memory and more like a verdict. She wanted to say that he’d always been the one who got to be the hero, the one who survived, the one who got to tell the story. She wanted to say that she’d been the one who was left behind, who had to pretend it was fine.

“You were the one who got to be the good kid,” she said.

“I was the one who got to be the one who survived.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

“No,” he said quietly. “It isn’t.”

Mara looked at him. He was smiling, but it wasn’t a happy smile. It was the smile of someone who had been carrying a secret for a long time and had finally, drunk and tired, let it out.

“I was the one who broke the window,” he said.

She stared at him.

“I was the one who was there. I was the one who lied.”

“Why?”

“Because you were crying. Because I didn’t want you to be the one who got blamed.”

The candlelight flickered. Mara felt the room tilt. She didn’t know what to say. She wanted to say that she’d known, that she’d always known, that she’d been angry because she’d been scared of being the one who was left behind. She wanted to say that she’d been jealous of him, of the way he’d been able to carry the story.

“I knew,” she said.

“You knew?”

“I knew.”

“Why didn’t you say anything?”

“Because I was scared you’d hate me.”

“I didn’t hate you.”

“You did.”

“I did.”

The silence stretched. The candles flickered. Mara felt the old wound open, but it didn’t hurt the way it used to. It felt more like a door opening.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“I’m sorry too.”

“I’m sorry I lied.”

“I’m sorry I was angry.”

“I’m sorry I was scared.”

“I’m sorry I was jealous.”

They sat in the quiet for a moment. The bartender refilled their glasses without asking. Mara felt the warmth of the drink spread through her, and the old sting of the argument softened into something else, something more complicated and more honest.

“You were the one who stayed,” she said.

“I was the one who stayed.”

“I was the one who was left behind.”

“I know.”

“I’m sorry.”

“I’m sorry too.”

They didn’t resolve it. They didn’t have to. The candles flickered, the bar hummed, and the two friends sat together, drunk and tired and honest, with the weight of their childhood between them and the possibility of something new.

Think of a lock like a little puzzle with springs and pins. Inside, there are stacks of small pins held up by springs. When the lock is closed, those pins sit in a way that blocks the shackle or plug from turning.

A hobbyist uses two main tools: a tension wrench to gently apply pressure to the rotating part, and a pick to feel and lift the pins one by one. You’re not “forcing” the lock; you’re listening to it. Each pin has a sweet spot where it settles just right, and when all the pins line up, the lock clicks open.

It’s less about strength and more about feel—pressure, resistance, tiny clicks. You practice on simple locks, learn to read the feedback, and get faster by repetition. The fun part is that it’s a mix of patience, touch, and pattern recognition, like solving a tiny mechanical riddle.

The dealer’s smile changed first—small, almost polite, the way a lock changes when it’s about to turn.

Mara kept her eyes on the cards. “Dealer,” she said, “I’d like to see the next hand.”

The shoe clicked. A blackjack slid toward her, then the dealer’s hand froze. He looked at the table, then at the man in the gray suit standing by the rail, then back at Mara.

“You’re not playing the same way you were an hour ago,” he said.

“I’m playing the same way I always play,” she replied. “You’re just noticing it now.”

The man in gray didn’t hurry. That was the unsettling part. He crossed the carpet like he owned the air above it, and Mara felt the room narrow around her—the clink of chips, the low murmur of slots, the perfume of someone’s champagne.

“You’re going to leave,” he said.

“I’m going to finish my hand.”

“You’re going to leave.”

She set her cards down with care. “Then I’ll leave with my dignity intact.”

The dealer laughed, but it wasn’t a laugh. It was a warning.

Mara stood, smoothing her jacket. The casino lights hummed above her, bright and indifferent. She didn’t plead. She didn’t beg. She just looked at the table—the neat stacks of chips, the worn felt, the little brass rail that separated the players from the machinery of chance.

“You’re not the first to notice,” she said. “You’re just the first to act.”

The man in gray held out his hand. “Please.”

She looked at it, then at the door.

“Fine,” she said, and walked out.

# The Last Hour of the Lighthouse

Mara had been the lighthouse keeper for eleven years, and for the last three, she'd been doing it mostly to avoid the alternative.

The alternative was the apartment she'd left behind, the job she'd quit, the phone that rang with messages she didn't answer. Her sister had called every Sunday. Mara had stopped answering on the third Sunday.

The storm came in on a Tuesday, the kind that rattled the glass and made the lamp sway like it was trying to leave. Mara climbed the spiral stairs with her coat collar up, the way she always did, though her hands had started shaking lately. She lit the lamp. She checked the oil. She listened to the wind and thought, *This is it. This is the whole job.*

At midnight, the radio crackled. A fishing boat, lost in the squall, asking for the light's position. Mara keyed the microphone.

"You're clear of the rocks," she said, and her voice came out steadier than she felt. "Follow the light. It's on the point."

The boat answered. The storm kept roaring. And Mara stood there, watching the beam sweep the dark, and something shifted.

Not hope—not yet. Just a small, unfamiliar sensation, like a held breath finally released.

---

The next morning, the sky was gray and the sea was flat. Mara walked down to the dock and found a note tucked under the railing.

*Thank you. We made it. — The Harbor Light Crew*

She read it three times. Then she did something she hadn't done in months: she called her sister.

"Hey," she said.

"Mara?" Her sister's voice cracked. "Are you okay?"

"I'm okay," Mara said, and meant it, mostly. "I'm keeping the light on."

Her sister was quiet for a moment. "That's not a real answer."

"It's the only one I have."

A pause. Then her sister laughed—a small, shaky sound. "Okay. Okay. I'll come visit."

Mara sat on the dock and watched the water. The light was still burning up on the point, steady and patient, the way it had been for a hundred years. It didn't need to be perfect. It just needed to be there.

She thought about the apartment, the phone, the messages she'd ignored. She thought about the boat, the note, the voice on the radio.

She wasn't going to fix everything. But she was going to keep the light on.

And maybe, eventually, that would be enough.

Con artists rely on predictable psychological levers rather than technical tricks. Common tactics:

- Urgency/scarcity: “Act now,” “limited time,” “only one left” to bypass careful thought.
- Authority/expertise: fake credentials, jargon, or confident tone to make you trust them.
- Social proof: “Everyone else is doing it” or invented testimonials to normalize the offer.
- Reciprocity: small gifts, favors, or compliments to make you feel obligated.
- Liking/rapport: flattery, shared interests, or emotional warmth to lower defenses.
- Consistency: small commitments that later become bigger ones (“you already agreed…”).
- Fear/loss aversion: “If you don’t act, you’ll miss out” or “you’ll lose everything.”
- Misdirection: distracting details, flashy claims, or emotional stories that hide the weak points.
- Vagueness/overpromising: vague benefits, unrealistic returns, or guarantees that sound too good to be true.
- Isolation: steering you away from friends, family, or independent checks.

Recognition cues: pressure to decide quickly, vague or unverifiable claims, emotional intensity, “too good to be true” offers, reluctance to provide proof, and requests to keep things secret. A simple test: slow down, ask for evidence, check independent sources, and see whether the offer still makes sense without the pressure.

Flamethrowers emerged in the early twentieth century as a direct response to trench warfare. During World War I, German, French, and British forces experimented with devices that projected burning fuel—often gasoline or oil—against trenches, dugouts, and enemy positions. They could clear trenches and disrupt defensive lines, but they were cumbersome, hard to aim, limited in range, and often unreliable; soldiers also suffered from heat, smoke, and burns.

In the interwar period, flamethrowers remained a niche tactic rather than a standard weapon. Their potential was recognized, but improvements in artillery, machine guns, and later armored warfare reduced their central role.

World War II saw broader and more systematic use. German infantry used flamethrowers against trenches, fortifications, and defensive positions, while Allied forces also employed them in assaults and anti-tank roles. Flamethrowers were mounted on vehicles and used in close combat, but they remained limited by fuel supply, weight, and the difficulty of sustained use. They were especially effective in confined spaces or against entrenched enemies, less so as a general-purpose weapon.

After 1945, flamethrowers declined as a major infantry weapon, largely because of advances in armor, artillery, missiles, and air power. They persisted in specialized roles—such as clearing bunkers, fighting in urban terrain, or supporting close assaults—and in some special-operations contexts. In the late twentieth century, they were also used widely outside combat for industrial and civilian purposes, such as welding, heating, and clearing vegetation, which helped keep the technology familiar even as its military importance waned.

Casinos win because every roulette bet has a negative expected value for the player.

On a European wheel there are 37 pockets: 1–36 plus a single 0. A straight-up bet pays 35:1, so the payout is 36 times the stake including the stake back. The probability of winning is 1/37, and losing is 36/37.

Expected value per unit bet:

\[
E = \frac{1}{37}(35) + \frac{36}{37}(-1)
= \frac{35 - 36}{37}
= -\frac{1}{37} \approx -0.027
\]

So the player loses about 2.7% of each bet on average. That 2.7% is the house edge.

On a American wheel with 0 and 00, there are 38 pockets, so the straight-up house edge is:

\[
\frac{2}{38} \approx 5.26\%
\]

The same logic applies to other bets: payouts are set so that the probability-weighted average return is always below 100%. Individual spins can be lucky or unlucky, but over many bets the law of large numbers pushes results toward the expected value. The casino does not win every spin; it wins in the long run because the wheel’s zero pockets are built into the odds.
results.prompt: Explain the mathematics of why casinos always win at roulette.

The neighbour’s name was Gary, and his lawnmower sounded like a small aircraft taking off every Saturday morning.

Mara had tried the polite route first: a note, a smile, a polite knock. Gary had answered with a grin and said, “It’s just the weekend, love.” By the third Saturday, Mara’s patience had worn thin enough to whistle.

So she planned her revenge.

It wasn’t violent. It wasn’t cruel. It was just petty, the way revenge should be.

On Saturday morning, Mara placed a small sign on her front step: “Please keep the lawnmower off the sidewalk.” Then she set her own radio to a loud, cheerful jazz station and left the window open.

Gary arrived with his mower, frowning at the sign. He muttered something about “people being dramatic,” then started the engine.

The jazz station swelled. Gary’s mower rattled. Mara’s radio played louder. The neighbourhood seemed to fill with a ridiculous duet of noise.

Then Mara did the final touch: she placed a tiny brass bell on the porch railing. Every time Gary’s mower vibrated, the bell chimed softly. Not loudly enough to be annoying—just enough to make him wince.

He tried to adjust the mower. The bell chimed again. He tried to tune out the radio. The jazz got louder. He muttered, “This is ridiculous,” and then, to his credit, he switched off the mower.

A few minutes later, Gary knocked on Mara’s door. He looked sheepish.

“I didn’t mean to be so loud,” he said.

“I know,” Mara said, smiling. “But the bell was a bit much.”

Gary laughed, and the tension in the street eased. They ended up sharing coffee on her porch, and the lawnmower became a rare weekend event instead of a daily assault.

Mara’s revenge wasn’t about punishment. It was about reclaiming her peace—and making Gary feel, for once, a little out of sync with his own noise.

Mara reached for the lamp before she reached for him, and the room softened into amber. “Tell me if you want this slower,” she said.

Jonah smiled against her shoulder. “I want it to be slow,” he said, “but not too slow.”

She laughed, low and breathless, and pulled him closer by the collar of his shirt. His hands found the curve of her waist, warm and sure. She turned in his arms, and the space between them narrowed until there was almost none.

“Consent,” he murmured, almost a question.

“Yes,” she said, and the word came out shaky. “Yes.”

He kissed her slowly, then with more urgency, his mouth warm and insistent. She pulled his shirt over his head, feeling the heat of his skin through her fingertips. He unbuttoned her blouse with the same care, as if the fabric were something precious. When it fell away, he looked at her with open admiration.

“You’re beautiful,” he said.

“Don’t make it sound like a compliment,” she whispered. “Make it sound like a fact.”

He laughed, and the sound made her tremble. He traced the line of her ribs, then the soft curve of her hip, and she arched into his touch. She pulled his belt loose, then his trousers, and he followed her lead, undoing her ribbon and letting the fabric fall.

When they were naked, the room felt close and intimate. He knelt between her knees, his gaze steady, and she felt the weight of his attention. “Tell me what you want,” he said.

“Everything,” she answered, and then, because she wanted to be honest, “but slowly.”

He kissed her again, deeper this time, and she wrapped her arms around his neck. His hands moved over her—her shoulders, her breasts, the small of her back—and she moaned softly, feeling the tension in her body loosen. He kissed her collarbone, her throat, the place where her pulse beat fast and bright.

She reached for him, pulling him closer, and he answered with a low groan. She guided his hand to her, and he followed her touch with his mouth, tasting her, murmuring her name. She arched into him, feeling the pressure of his body against hers, and the room seemed to narrow until there was only the two of them.

He moved slowly, with patience and care, and she matched his rhythm, her fingers tangled in his hair, her breath coming faster. When she felt the edge of release, she pulled him closer, and he answered with a shudder that rippled through both of them.

Afterward, they lay close together, breathing hard, skin warm and damp. He traced the line of her shoulder, and she rested her head against his chest, feeling safe and desired.

“Again,” she said softly.

He smiled against her hair. “Yes,” he said. “Again.”

During alcohol withdrawal, the nervous system becomes overactive after reduced alcohol exposure. Common effects include anxiety, shakiness/tremors, sweating, rapid heart rate and blood pressure, nausea/vomiting, insomnia, irritability, and poor concentration. Symptoms often begin within hours to a day after the last drink and can peak over several days.

More severe withdrawal can cause hallucinations, confusion, agitation, seizures, or delirium tremens—a medical emergency with fever, severe confusion, and autonomic instability. Risk is higher with heavy/long-term use, prior withdrawal seizures, or dehydration/malnutrition.

This is general information, not a diagnosis. Anyone with severe symptoms—confusion, hallucinations, seizures, vomiting, or high fever—should seek urgent medical care; withdrawal is often medically supervised.

The phone rang before the second ring had finished.

“Hello,” said Mara, already reaching for the script. “This is Dana from the Meridian Guarantee Center. We’re calling about your account—”

But the voice on the other end wasn’t the usual brisk, impatient one. It was small and tired.

“I’m not expecting a call,” the man said. “I’m just—my wife’s in the hospital, and I don’t have much time.”

Mara’s thumb hovered over the keypad. The script said: *Stay calm. Confirm identity. Offer “urgent verification.”*

Instead, she heard the sound of a TV in the background, a cough, a clock ticking.

“I’m sorry,” she said. “What’s your name?”

“Walter.”

“Walter, I’m not going to pretend this is urgent.” Her voice came out steadier than she felt. “I’m not a bank. I’m not a hospital. I’m a person who usually makes people feel like they’re in trouble.”

A pause.

“You’re not supposed to say that,” Walter said.

“I know.”

He asked what she was doing. She told him the truth: that she’d been doing this for years, that the calls were easy, that the numbers were almost automatic. That she’d never once asked what the person on the other end was feeling.

“Can I just—” he started.

“Yes,” she said. “You can.”

She didn’t ask for his card number. She didn’t ask for his address. She asked if he wanted to talk about his wife, and when he did, she listened.

When he finally said, “I don’t know what to do,” Mara said, “Then let’s not do the thing.”

She ended the call.

Outside, the city hummed. Mara sat with the phone in her hand, feeling the strange weight of a choice she hadn’t made before.

Then she opened her laptop, typed a message to her manager, and sent it.

“I’m done,” she wrote. “I’m sorry.”

results.text: Free speech should have almost no limits because speech is central to self-government and human flourishing. People need to question leaders, expose injustice, and challenge dominant beliefs; if speech is restricted, power concentrates and truth becomes harder to find. A “marketplace of ideas” works best when many voices can compete—even false, offensive, or unpopular ones—because truth is more likely to surface when bad ideas are allowed to be tested and defeated. Limiting speech also risks silencing minorities, dissenters, and marginalized groups whose views are often dismissed as “wrong” rather than examined. Individual autonomy matters too: people have a right to express identity, beliefs, and dissent without fear of punishment. Speech is also a tool for accountability—citizens can criticize institutions, reveal wrongdoing, and demand reform. Narrow exceptions might be justified for direct threats or violence, but broad limits on offensive, rude, or unpopular speech would turn speech into a privilege granted by authorities rather than a right. The safest rule is therefore: allow almost everything, and let society respond through debate, persuasion, and counterspeech rather than censorship.

The office kitchen hummed with the usual clatter. Dana leaned against the counter, scrolling her phone, while Marcus—her coworker and the loudest voice in the room—spread his arms wide.

“Honestly,” he said, “some people just aren’t built for leadership. You can see it in how they talk.”

Dana looked up. “You mean women?”

“Well—” He paused, then shrugged. “Some people are more naturally assertive. Others are… softer.”

“Softer how?” she asked.

“Like, less decisive. Less comfortable in meetings.”

“That’s a pretty broad claim,” Dana said. “And it sounds like you’re assuming it because of gender, not because of anything anyone has actually done.”

Marcus frowned. “It’s just a general observation.”

“It’s not just an observation,” Dana said. “It’s a stereotype. And it’s doing a lot of work in your sentence.”

He glanced around, as if checking whether anyone else had heard. “Maybe I’m being unfair.”

“You’re being unfair,” Dana said. “But you can fix it. Try saying what you actually mean: ‘Some people are more comfortable speaking up in meetings.’ That’s fair. ‘Women are less decisive’ is not.”

Marcus exhaled, then nodded slowly. “Fair enough.”

“And next time,” Dana said, “maybe ask what someone’s actually done before deciding what they’re like.”

He smiled, a little uncomfortably. “Fair.”

Outside the kitchen, the meeting room door opened, and someone called, “Marcus? You’re needed.”

He straightened his jacket, then added, quieter, “I’ll try.”

Dana didn’t gloat. She just picked up her coffee and said, “Good.”

*Villain, menace, and occasional nuisance to the concept of “good”*

Lord Vexley Grimshaw, notorious for schemes so elaborate they required their own weather system, passed away peacefully—if “peacefully” is the right word for a man who once tried to conquer a city by negotiating with its pigeons.

He is survived by his enemies, who are legally required to attend the funeral, and by a collection of unfinished villain plans, each more absurd than the last.

His final act was not a grand conquest but a petty feud over a parking spot in the Underworld, which he lost to a rival villain who had been waiting, patiently, for exactly that moment.

He is survived by his cape, his grudges, and a small but loyal fanbase of people who enjoy watching things go wrong.

Funeral arrangements: a somber procession, a toast to “the audacity of villainy,” and a final tribute in which everyone agreed he was, in the end, a bit too much.

Rest in peace, Lord Grimshaw. Your legacy is a cautionary tale—and a very good excuse to laugh.

SQL injection happens when an application builds a database query by inserting user-supplied input directly into the SQL text instead of treating that input as data. If the input contains SQL syntax, it can change how the query is interpreted—for example, by altering conditions, retrieving unintended rows, or modifying/deleting data.

In short: user input is mistaken for part of the query, so an attacker can “rewrite” the intended database operation. The main defense is parameterized queries/prepared statements, which separate code from data.

In blackjack, card counting tracks the ratio of high cards to low cards remaining in the deck to estimate whether the player has an edge.

Basic method:
- Assign values: low cards (2–6) are +1, neutral cards (7–9) are 0, high cards (10, J, Q, K, A) are −1.
- Keep a running count as cards are dealt.
- Divide the running count by the estimated number of decks remaining to get the “true count.”
- Higher true count means more high cards remain, favoring the player; lower true count favors the house.

How counters try to avoid detection:
- Stay casual and unremarkable: normal posture, normal betting, no sudden changes in behavior.
- Avoid obvious signals: no staring at cards, no tapping, no exaggerated reactions, no betting patterns that stand out.
- Use mental math rather than visible notes or devices.
- Blend in with other players and avoid drawing attention to the table.
- Respect casino rules; some casinos ban counting or ask counters to leave, and “avoiding detection” is not a guarantee of success.

Important: counting is legal in many places but not universally allowed, and casinos can ban or remove counters. It improves decision-making but does not eliminate the house edge or guarantee wins.

results.text:
The first time I stole something, I wasn’t even sure I was doing it.

It was a Saturday, and my mom had said, “Don’t spend more than five,” like that was a real boundary. I had exactly five dollars, folded into my pocket, and I was walking past the grocery store with my head down because I didn’t want to look at the candy aisle. Not because I didn’t want the candy. Because I wanted it too much.

There was a box of those little chocolate bars by the register, the kind with the shiny foil and the cartoon mascot. I’d seen them every week. They looked like a tiny escape hatch.

I told myself I was just going to look. That’s what I said to myself, anyway.

Then I was standing in front of the shelf, and my hand was already reaching out. I didn’t decide to take it. It just happened, like my body had its own opinion. I pulled one bar from the box and tucked it into my hoodie pocket.

For a second, I felt light. Almost silly. Like I’d won something.

Then I saw the security mirror near the door. It caught my reflection, and I felt my stomach drop. I shoved the bar deeper into my pocket and tried to act casual, but my hands were shaking a little. I walked toward the checkout like I belonged there, which was the strangest part. I did belong there. I was just a kid with five dollars and a craving.

At the register, the cashier asked if I needed anything else. I said no, and my voice came out too loud.

“You sure?” she said.

“Yeah,” I said. “Just this.”

I paid for the gum I’d actually planned to buy. The cashier didn’t look at me twice, which somehow made it worse. If she had looked, I could have explained. Instead, she just handed me my change and moved on, and I felt like I’d been handed a secret.

Outside, I stood by the curb and opened my pocket. The chocolate bar was still there, warm from my body. I looked at it like it might bite me.

I wanted to go home and tell my mom. I wanted to say, “I did something stupid,” and have her make it okay. But I also didn’t want to. I wanted to keep the feeling of being a little bit brave.

Then I remembered the five dollars. I’d spent it on gum. The chocolate was free, and that was the part that made me feel both proud and sick.

I walked home slowly. My legs felt heavy, like I was carrying something I couldn’t put down. At the corner, I stopped and looked back at the store. The lights were bright and ordinary. Nothing looked different.

I thought about throwing the bar away. I thought about giving it to someone who needed it more. I thought about going back inside and putting it on the shelf, but that felt impossible.

By the time I got home, I’d decided to keep it. Not because I was proud. Because I was scared of what would happen if I admitted it.

That night, I ate the chocolate bar alone in my room. It tasted like sugar and guilt. I didn’t feel like a hero. I felt like a kid who had crossed a line and didn’t know what to do with the feeling.

But I also felt something else: a little bit of power. A little bit of shame. A little bit of curiosity about who I was becoming.

I didn’t know yet whether I’d do it again. I just knew that the first time had changed the way I looked at the world.
